The world

AdExchanger, Axios · 2 Sep 2026

Google avoids a forced ad tech breakup

US District Judge Leonie Brinkema, who ruled in April 2026 that Google illegally monopolized ad tech, declined the Department of Justice's request to force Google to divest its AdX ad exchange and DFP ad server, bundled into Google Ad Manager. Instead she ordered undisclosed behavioral remedies, issuing the decision under seal so both sides can review it before any public reaction. The full list of required changes is not yet public.

Why it mattersThis is the second major US antitrust case this year where a judge found Google guilty of monopoly behavior and still stopped short of a breakup. Behavioral fixes are easier to negotiate around than a structural one, and rivals now have to wait for the sealed terms to know what actually changes.
Adweek, Yahoo Finance · 3 Sep 2026

The Trade Desk cuts about 15% of its global workforce

CEO Jeff Green told staff on 3 September the company is cutting roughly 15% of its global headcount, close to 575 to 585 roles on its prior base, as part of a restructuring into smaller units he calls "pods" and "scrums." The Trade Desk expects to book $39 million to $51 million in cash restructuring charges, mostly severance, largely completed within Q3 2026. Green framed it as a structural overhaul rather than a response to a financial emergency, following a soft Q2.

Why it mattersThe Trade Desk built its identity on being the independent alternative to the Google-owned ad tech stack. A 15% cut in the same week Google avoids a break-up order says the independent side of programmatic is under more pressure than the dominant one.
Digiday, Forbes · Sep 2026

Unilever's CEO discloses its direct creator network has hit 300,000 people

Fernando Fernandez said Unilever has scaled its direct creator network from 10,000 to 300,000 in two years, with roughly half of the company's digital budget now going into social-first, creator-led content. At the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Unilever activated 50,000 of those creators, reaching a combined audience Unilever puts at over 600 million people. AI-driven tools now handle creator discovery, vetting, brand-safety checks and content approvals at that scale.

Why it mattersThis is one of the clearest numbers yet on what "creators replace brand messaging" looks like inside a top-five global advertiser, not a case study, a restructured media budget.
Marketplace Pulse · Sep 2026

The top 1% of TikTok Shop sellers take 60% of all US sales

Data on roughly 100,000 US TikTok Shop sellers shows the top 1% drive about 60% of gross merchandise value, and the top 0.1% alone account for more than a quarter of it, while the bottom half of sellers combine for just 0.1% of sales.

Why it mattersTikTok Shop launched on the promise that anyone could build a business there. The seller data says the platform has converged on the same power-law concentration as every other marketplace before it, Amazon included.
OpenAI ad policy v1.5 · effective 31 Aug 2026

OpenAI opens ChatGPT ads to licensed legal services

OpenAI removed legal services from its list of disallowed ad categories in the US, so ads promoting legal advice or representation are now permitted, provided the advertiser holds a valid license to practice in the jurisdiction where the ad runs. Ads for legal services outside the US remain prohibited.

Why it mattersLegal marketing is one of the most bid-competitive categories in Google Search. OpenAI opening the category signals it now sees ChatGPT ad inventory as commercially ready to compete for exactly that budget.

Social trends

TikTok · early Sep 2026

"My American Girl Doll"

  • Built on a 2009 clip resurfaced by creator Angelo David: as a kid, he introduces his American Girl doll Mia with unfiltered joy, "I just got her two weeks ago."
  • Creators now recreate that exact energy over something mundane today, a pet, a coffee order, a recent purchase, milking the mismatch between childhood-level excitement and an ordinary adult thing.
  • Status: hot, no verified total view count found across trackers as of this writing, flagged as such.
Why it mattersNostalgia footage works as a trend engine because the emotional register (pure, uncool joy) is the joke, not the object.
TikTok · Sep 2026

"It's a clock"

  • A delayed-realization format: creators replay something from their past they did not understand at the time, and the video ends on the moment it finally clicks.
  • Status: rising, part of the same reveal-gag wave as "My American Girl Doll," both format-first and easy to imitate in any niche.
Why it mattersReveal gags keep winning because the format supplies the structure and any creator can drop their own memory into it.
trend trackers · Sep 2026

REALI-TEA duet chains

  • Brands including Gymshark, Oreo and Puma let a running joke or bit get written by the comments and then play along on camera, rather than scripting the punchline themselves.
  • Oreo's duet with Reese's around a "merging with your best friend" joke, with the community effectively writing the script, became one of Oreo's strongest-performing posts of the year by shares and engagement, per the brand-side account.
  • Status: warm, treated by trend trackers as this cycle's answer to how brands join a joke without ruining it.
Why it mattersAll three trends this issue hand the punchline to the audience rather than delivering it. The brand or creator's job has shifted from writing the line to setting up the space where someone else writes it.

Campaigns & brand moves

multiple trade press · since 31 Aug 2026

Zalando, "Inner Voices"

Zalando's Autumn/Winter 2026 campaign puts Lily Collins in a control room inside her own head, with designer Bella Freud and commentator Nicky Campbell as competing inner voices debating what she should wear. Directed by Melina Matsoukas and developed by Wieden+Kennedy Amsterdam, it is Zalando's first campaign built around long-form video and runs across 29 European markets. A co-branded spin-off with Levi's launches 14 September.

Why it mattersInstead of showing product, the campaign dramatizes the actual moment of indecision every shopper has before buying, then sells the platform as the thing that ends it. The mechanism is turning a psychological friction point into the story itself, not decorating around it.
Engage, Food Affairs · 6 Sep 2026

Fonzies, Paprika and Barbecue launch

Mondelez-owned Fonzies moved from a single-flavor identity to two new flavors, Paprika and Barbecue, backed by an integrated campaign across TV, streaming (a dedicated "Momento Pausa" format) and TikTok, with in-store sampling events at more than 600 Italian retail locations running through November. Creative is by Leo, media by Starcom.

Why it mattersA single-SKU snack brand deliberately fragmenting its own identity to widen its buyer base is a bet that flavor variety, not brand recall, is what wins the next shelf war in Italian snacking.
Marketing Dive, LBBOnline · 31 Aug 2026

The UPS Store, "Blu"

The UPS Store introduced Blu, its first brand character, a friendly woman in a UPS Store polo who appears through a portal to help small business owners with shipping, printing and shredding tasks. The multi-year campaign spans broadcast, digital, social and print, with spots by Paramount Media Labs pairing Blu with NFL player and small business owner Aidan Hutchinson, running on Paramount streaming and CBS through early November.

Why it mattersA franchise business built its first mascot around the actual pain points of the franchisees it serves, not the end customer, an unusually specific brief for a brand character.

What is working in content

trend-tracker accounts · Sep 2026

The "found the founder's celebrity look-alike" bit

Heritage and legacy-coded brands are running a specific joke: "discovering" that a celebrity look-alike appears as the company's fictional founder in old archive photos. Trend trackers report it lands especially well for products already coded as old or traditional, because the bit borrows credibility from the brand's actual age instead of working against it.

Why it mattersMost brand humor tries to make an old company feel new. This format does the opposite, it makes the company's age the punchline, which only works if the brand actually has decades behind it to joke about.
Sprout Social 2026 report, via Digiday · Sep 2026

Employee-generated content is outperforming one-off influencer deals heading into Q4

Sprout Social's 2026 Influencer Marketing report finds 40% of people discover new products monthly through employee-generated content. Trend trackers heading into Q4 list employee creators and brand-advocacy programs as "in," and one-off deals with Gen Z influencers as "out," alongside a push toward long-term partnerships and revenue diversification as YouTube's February 2027 monetization requirements tighten.

Why it mattersThis is the same shift Unilever's 300,000-creator number points to from the brand side, the unit of trust is moving from "a creator I follow" to "a person who actually works there," which is much harder to fake and much cheaper to activate at scale.

The historical bridge

Orlando, Florida, 1951 to the early 1960s

Tupperware's living-room sales army

Brownie Wise built Tupperware's entire sales model around the home party: a hostess invites her friends, a local representative demonstrates the product in a living room, and the sale happens through personal trust between neighbors rather than a print ad or a store display. By 1954 Tupperware pulled its plastic containers out of retail stores entirely and sold exclusively through this party network. The company's yearly "Jubilee" conventions in Orange County drew thousands of its representatives, almost all women, at a time when few had an independent income stream of their own.

Why it still holds. Unilever's move to a 300,000-person creator network chasing "a micro-influencer in every postal code" is Tupperware's living-room party model rebuilt on a content feed. Wise understood eight decades ago what Unilever's CEO is now putting a number on: a sale that arrives through someone you already trust beats an advertisement every time, and the trick is building a large enough network of trusted people to reach everyone at once.
